findings.text: The first paragraph does its job. A newcomer learns what Athena is, who it is for, and what problem it solves before reading anything else.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The one section that could show Athena's promise in action (models, verdict, cost) shows an error message instead. It sits near the top, so a newcomer's first proof is a failure, and the page never shows them a traced commit.
findings.source: Heading "Check it on a real job": "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: Someone who came to learn about Athena gets a page that is almost entirely about a different project, firstmate. The page explains why it does this, but most of the text (states, transitions, design choices, 45 claims) does not tell them anything about Athena itself.
findings.source: Title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and "This page is that study of firstmate."

findings.text: The "Start here" section asks the reader to learn seven firstmate-specific terms before the first walkthrough. Some definitions admit they are incomplete ("this page gives no test for it"), which makes the section heavy going for a newcomer.
findings.source: Heading "Start here" and "Words used first": "captain", "yolo", "in scope", "green", "red", "local-only landing", "home"

findings.text: Several glossary entries say the term is undefined. That is honest, but it makes the page harder to read and leaves gaps a newcomer cannot fill.
findings.source: Glossary entries such as "The firstmate source does not define a captain call." and "The firstmate source does not define a durable record."

findings.text: The next steps are concrete and in order: what you need first, how to clone, how to install, and a first command with a note on what it acts on. A newcomer knows exactly what to do next, and the top of the page links straight to this section.
findings.source: Heading "Next steps": "git clone https://github.com/doodla/athena.git", "./setup.sh", "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The page says Athena uses one AI model to do the work and a different one to check it. It never says which accounts, API keys or costs a newcomer needs before running `athena ask`.
findings.source: Prerequisites list: "Claude Code, or npm to install it."

findings.text: This link in the header is for the project owner, not a first-time visitor. It sits right next to the newcomer's "Next step" link and could confuse them.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Every statement links to a claim, and every claim links to lines in firstmate's files at a fixed commit. This is the clearest evidence on the page that Athena does what it says about tracing its work.
findings.source: "Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it; the claims, with links to their sources, are listed at the end."
